title: France's most famous pastry started out Austrian

segments.text: France's most famous pastry started out Austrian.
segments.note: Hook: breaks a belief in under 3 seconds.

segments.text: And the man who brought it to Paris wasn't a baker. He was a soldier.
segments.note: Open loop, paid off at t06-t07.

segments.text: Long before the croissant, Vienna had the kipfel: a soft little bread roll shaped like a crescent moon.
Legend says bakers invented it after saving the city from an enemy army. Danger, heroes, breakfast. Great story.
Not true. The roll was already hundreds of years old.
So how did it get to France? Enter the soldier.
In the 1830s, August Zang, an ex-army officer from Vienna, opened a bakery in Paris. Business boomed.
French bakers copied his roll and named it after its shape. Croissant. Crescent.
But here's the twist: it still wasn't flaky. It was just bread.
Then French bakers tried something. Fold butter into the dough. Roll. Fold again. And again.
One layer of butter becomes twenty-seven. In the oven, steam blows them apart.
That shatter when you bite in? That's the French part.
